strengths: The paper offers a well-motivated extension of classifier-based Bayesian optimization using label propagation and label spreading. Supporting both sampled unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools makes the combination relevant to several optimization settings.

The experiments cover synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, architecture search, and an image-based search task. Twenty repetitions with standard errors provide meaningful empirical evidence, with particularly promising improvements over BORE and LFBO on synthetic functions and NATS-Bench.

The appendices examine kernel bandwidth, sampling distributions, unlabeled sample counts, threshold ratios, and pool subsampling. These studies expose useful parameter sensitivities and computational tradeoffs. The background and pseudocode also make the overall approach understandable.
weaknesses: The central benefit of semi-supervised learning is insufficiently isolated. Figure 12 includes a useful comparison without unlabeled data, but fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main experiments learn beta. The comparison without unlabeled data sometimes performs substantially better, including on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. A kernel-only baseline with comparable bandwidth selection and identical acquisition optimization and tie-breaking is needed to establish whether label propagation itself explains the main gains. This unresolved attribution substantially weakens the contribution.

The justification for the sampling strategy overstates what is established. Gaussian samples centered on evaluated inputs do not ensure that high-density regions share the same threshold-defined label. Likewise, expanding the region assigned high improvement probability does not by itself demonstrate better exploration. Appendix D acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. semi-supervised learning bounds do not apply directly to adaptive Bayesian optimization; the proposed mechanism therefore remains largely heuristic.

Important implementation details remain unspecified, including input scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping parameters, beta optimization bounds and initialization, and complete baseline training settings. Acquisition optimization over finite pools and handling previously evaluated candidates also need clarification. These choices materially affect the reported comparisons and impede reproduction.

The evidence for difficult high-dimensional optimization is limited. All continuous synthetic functions are two-dimensional, while the 64-dimensional MNIST embeddings come from a network trained to predict the same three-digit labels that define the objective. This supplies substantial objective-specific information. Comparing against directly ranking candidates using that network's predictions would help establish the benchmark's difficulty and the optimizer's added value.

The practical computational tradeoff is incompletely evaluated. Figure 14 varies pool size using fixed beta and does not compare end-to-end runtime against the baselines. The main method additionally optimizes beta every iteration and uses 1,000 acquisition-optimization initializations, so the computational cost accompanying its evaluation-efficiency gains remains unclear.

A smaller mathematical correction is needed in Section 4.1: the definition of p_ij uses column normalization, implying P = W D^{-1} for symmetric W, but the text states P = D^{-1}W. This must be reconciled with the transpose in Equation 11 so that the intended propagation update is unambiguous.
